At the agri-startup fair in the district hall, fans creaking overhead, Deepak had eight minutes on stage for his banana-ripening chambers. His last slide was the one he was proudest of: revenue doubling every quarter for three years, ending in a tall green bar.
In the question round, Zubin, who had backed three cold-storage companies, raised a hand. "Doubling every quarter. Based on what? How many chambers are running now?"
"Four."
"And how many farmers have paid twice?"
"Two... but the demand is huge."
"Then why double and not triple? Or halve?" Zubin asked, not unkindly. "If this slide is a guess, I have to wonder which of the others are too."
The hall went quiet. Deepak's ears burned. After the session, two investors who had been nodding earlier left without taking his card.

Mahima's investor meetings in Bengaluru were going well, and everyone kept saying, "We'll close in six weeks." Her mentor, Hansa, laughed when she heard. "Everyone says six weeks. Plan for six months. And plan for never."
That night in her Koramangala flat, Mahima opened a blank sheet and made three columns.
Case A: money arrives in three months. Hire two engineers in April as planned.
Case B: money arrives in six months. Freeze hiring; she and her co-founder take half salaries from May; drop the paid design tool.
Case C: no money at all. By July, shrink to the two founders and one support person, move to a cheaper co-working seat, and focus only on paying customers.
Beside each case she wrote the date on which she would switch. When April came with only "positive noises" from investors, she didn't panic. She moved to Case B that Monday.

qa.a: Freeze hiring, take half salaries from May and drop the paid design tool.

qa.q: How did Mahima feel when April came with only positive noises?
qa.a: She stayed calm instead of panicking, because the switch to Case B was already planned.

qa.q: What else could strengthen Mahima's plan?
qa.a: Sharing the three cases with her co-founder and team early, so any switch doesn't come as a shock.

Shreya's diary, Sunday.
Two offers on the table and my head is spinning. Offer one is bigger: a higher valuation, the kind of number you'd brag about. Offer two is smaller.
But tonight I made a list instead of just staring at the headline.
Board seats: offer one wants two seats on a board of three. They could outvote us. Offer two wants one seat, and only as an observer for the first year.
Liquidation preference: under offer one, if we sell, they get twice their money back before anyone else. Offer two, just once.
Help: I called three founders each fund had backed. Offer one's founders were polite but vague. Offer two's founders all said the same thing: "They picked up the phone when things went wrong."
Arohi, my co-founder, says the big number is tempting, and she's not wrong. But I'll ask our lawyer to explain both on Tuesday before we choose.

Mentor's note, 12 September.
I went with Jatin today to the startup lawyer he had hired to go through the shareholder agreement before signing. He had printed all forty pages and marked every clause he didn't understand in yellow. There was a lot of yellow.
The lawyer took two hours and explained each marked clause in plain language: what the investors' approval rights would mean in practice, what would happen to his shares if he left early, how a future sale would be split. She was careful to say this was a general explanation of how such terms usually work, and that Jatin should ask again if anything changed.
Jatin asked good questions, including two he admitted felt "stupid". On the way out he said he had been close to signing last week on trust. We agreed he would send the lawyer's notes to his co-founder before any decision.
— Vaibhav

Pranav, the first thing I did after the layoff wasn't updating my CV. It was a sheet of paper. I'm Salma, and I needed to know how long I actually had. So I wrote down every monthly cost: rent, the scooter EMI, the money I send home to Ammi, groceries, phone. Then what I had: my savings plus the severance, which HR had finally explained properly. I divided one by the other. Five and a half months.
Then I looked for leaks. Three streaming plans, a music plan, a gym I wasn't using. I cancelled all but one. That added about three weeks.
So I had a date: mid-November. Everything in my job search was planned around it. If nothing by September, I'd widen the search to other cities. Having a date made me less frantic, not more. Before, the fear had no edges.

After the layoff, my first instinct was to beg: "Hi, do you have a job for me?" Bhavna, my old team lead, talked me out of it over coffee. "Thomas, ask people for advice, not jobs. Advice is easy to give."
So I listed twenty people I had actually worked with over five years: testers, managers, the product person who left for a health startup. To each I wrote a short, personal message: how they were, what I'd been working on, and one question. "Do you know any teams that are growing and might need someone who builds data pipelines?"
Seventeen replied. Most had ideas, not openings. But four said, "Actually, my team is hiring. Can I refer you?" Those four referrals became four interviews in three weeks.
I had sent zero applications through job portals.

qa.q: How was Sharmila feeling when she came to the week 3 session?
qa.a: Sharmila was discouraged after forty online applications with no response.

qa.q: What made the outreach messages work?
qa.a: They were personal, rewritten until they sounded like her, and asked about growing teams rather than begging for a job.

qa.q: How does Chandrika see Sharmila's progress?
qa.a: Chandrika sees her move from discouraged to hopeful, with referrals and interviews lined up.

grounding: It shows a laid-off woman writing to former colleagues for advice on which teams are hiring, instead of asking for jobs, and getting four referrals that lead to interviews.
